passage:
Monday night.

Results came out. I missed the engineering entrance cutoff again, second time. Aadhya called, and I couldn't even speak properly.

Spent the evening lying on the roof, staring at the water tank, feeling like the biggest failure in the colony. Mummy left dinner outside my door. I didn't eat for a while.

Around eleven I finally opened my mock test sheets. And I saw it: maths was fine, physics was fine, chemistry was a disaster both years. It's not that I'm stupid. It's one subject I kept avoiding.

I'm going to try one more time. Not the same way. Chemistry first, every morning. I'll ask Aadhya's cousin for her notes.

I'm scared to fail again. But I'm more scared of never finding out.

Chetan

qa.q: Which subject did Chetan see was the weak one in both years?
qa.a: Chemistry.

qa.q: What does Chetan mean by being more scared of never finding out?
qa.a: Chetan is afraid of failing again, but would regret giving up more, so chooses to try instead of quitting.

qa.q: Which part of Chetan's new plan shows a lesson learned from the setback?
qa.a: Tackling chemistry first every morning, because it targets the actual reason for missing the cutoff.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when Chetan says they're trying again?
qa.a: Aadhya would probably be relieved and proud after hearing Chetan unable to speak on the phone, and glad to help with the notes.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows the writer finding the grit to try again after a major setback, with a smarter plan.

passage:
Gargi: the stall's shutting down
Indu: what?? the momo stall?
Gargi: rent went up and I was losing money every week. 6 months of savings gone
Indu: oh Gargi 😢
Gargi: I sat in the empty stall for an hour today. felt like everyone was right, I'm not a business person
Indu: that's not true. people LOVED the momos
Indu: what actually went wrong?
Gargi: honestly? the location. no evening crowd
Gargi: and I bought too much stock
Indu: so it's not you, it's the plan
Gargi: ...maybe
Gargi: the college canteen is looking for a food vendor. less rent. evening crowd
Indu: DO IT
Gargi: I'm scared. but I'm writing the proposal tonight
Indu: that's the Gargi I know 👏

qa.q: What kind of food did Gargi sell at the stall?
qa.a: Momos.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel sitting in the empty stall?
qa.a: Gargi felt crushed and ashamed, thinking the failure proved Gargi wasn't a business person.

qa.q: What helped Gargi move toward trying again?
qa.a: Indu's question about what went wrong helped Gargi see specific fixable causes, making a better attempt possible to plan.

qa.q: How might Indu feel when Gargi decides to write the proposal?
qa.a: Indu is clearly excited and proud, seeing a friend's determination return.

grounding: Shows a young adult building the grit to try again after a business failure, helped by a friend.

passage: At the village akhada, the red earth was still marked from yesterday's district bout. Vijay, twenty-one, had lost in the final round, pinned in under a minute in front of the whole village. That night he didn't go home. He sat by the pit until his coach, Omkar ustad, found him. "Shame?" asked Omkar. Vijay nodded. "Everyone saw." "Everyone saw you get there too," Omkar said. "Why did you lose?" Vijay thought. "I rushed. I got tired too early." "So?" Vijay stood up, brushed the earth off his legs. "So I train stamina. Morning runs to the canal and back." At dawn the next day, the village milkman saw him running past the fields, alone, his breath clouding in the cold.

qa.q: Where did the milkman see Vijay running at dawn?
qa.a: Past the fields.

qa.q: How was Vijay feeling after losing the bout?
qa.a: He felt ashamed because the whole village had watched him lose.

qa.q: What did Omkar's questions help Vijay do?
qa.a: They helped him find the real reason he lost and turn his shame into a concrete training plan.

qa.q: How might the milkman see Vijay running alone at dawn?
qa.a: He might be surprised and impressed that the boy who lost is already back at work.

grounding: Shows a young wrestler in a village finding the grit to train again after a public defeat.

passage: Javier, twenty-one, read the results on the board outside the training centre in Valencia twice before it sank in: failed again, the second time, by four points. He walked out and sat on the curb in the heat. His friend Chen, who had passed, sat down beside him without saying anything about his own result. 'I'm done,' Javier said. 'My uncle was right. I should just keep stacking boxes at the warehouse.' Chen waited. After a while Javier pulled the marked paper from his bag and looked at it properly. Almost all his mistakes were in the circuit calculations, not the practical. 'It's always the same section,' he muttered. That evening he taped the paper above his bed and asked Chen for his old calculation notes. The next exam was in March. He wrote the date on his hand.

qa.q: By how many points did Javier fail?
qa.a: Four points.

qa.q: Why did Javier say 'I'm done' at first?
qa.a: He felt crushed and discouraged after failing twice and was echoing his uncle's doubts.

qa.q: What turned Javier's setback into a plan?
qa.a: Looking closely at the marked paper showed his mistakes were in one section, which gave him a clear target to study.

qa.q: Why might Chen have said nothing about his own result?
qa.a: He sensed Javier's pain and chose to support him quietly rather than highlight his own pass.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding the grit to try again after a second failed exam.

passage: At the district sports hostel, the track lights came on at six. Sangeeta, twenty, had missed selection for the state relay team by one-tenth of a second, two weeks after coming back from a hamstring injury. For three days she didn't come to practice. On the fourth, Coach Manjula found her sitting in the stands. 'You can quit,' the coach said evenly. 'Nobody will blame you.' Sangeeta was quiet for a long time. 'If I quit now, the injury decides. I want to decide.' She laced her spikes. The first two starts were ugly; her leg felt stiff and her face burned with embarrassment in front of the juniors. On the third, she found her rhythm again. Coach Manjula wrote the next trial date on the whiteboard and underlined it twice.

qa.q: By how much did Sangeeta miss selection?
qa.a: By one-tenth of a second.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta mean by 'I want to decide'?
qa.a: She felt determined not to let the injury and setback end her running for her; she wanted to choose to keep trying.

qa.q: What was wise about the coach saying 'You can quit'?
qa.a: It removed pressure and let Sangeeta find her own reason to continue, which makes her determination stronger.

qa.q: How might the juniors see Sangeeta's ugly starts?
qa.a: They might notice her struggling, but also learn that senior athletes keep going after setbacks.

grounding: Illustrates a young athlete building the resolve to return to training after a painful setback.
